Here are the **2026 IRA Maximum Contribution Limits**, as officially announced by the IRS in November 2025:

## 2026 IRA Contribution Limits

| Age Group | Annual Contribution Limit |
|---|---|
| **Under age 50** | **$7,500** |
| **Age 50–59** | **$8,600** (includes $1,100 catch-up) |
| **Age 60–63** | **$8,600** (super catch-up — same as 50+) |
| **Age 64 and older** | **$8,600** (includes $1,100 catch-up) |

> These limits apply to the **combined total** across all your IRAs (Traditional, Roth, or both). You cannot exceed the limit by contributing to multiple accounts.

### Key Changes from 2025

The base contribution limit **increased from $7,000 to $7,500**, and the catch-up contribution for those age 50 and older **increased from $1,000 to $1,100** (a change introduced by the SECURE 2.0 Act, which now indexes the catch-up amount to inflation).

### Income Limits for Roth IRA Eligibility (2026)

Your ability to contribute to a **Roth IRA** is subject to income (MAGI) thresholds:

| Filing Status | Full Contribution | Phase-Out Range | No Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Single / Head of Household** | Under $153,000 | $153,000 – $168,000 | $168,000+ |
| **Married Filing Jointly** | Under $242,000 | $242,000 – $252,000 | $252,000+ |

### Important Notes

- **Traditional IRA** contributions are always allowed regardless of income, but the **deductibility** may be limited if you (or your spouse) are covered by a workplace retirement plan.
- The contribution limit is also capped at your **taxable compensation for the year** if it is less than the dollar limit.
- The deadline to make 2026 IRA contributions is **April 15, 2027** (Tax Day).

**Sources:** [IRS Official Announcement](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/401k-limit-increases-to-24500-for-2026-ira-limit-increases-to-7500) | [IRS Retirement Topics – IRA Contribution Limits](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits)
